headline: Rattlesnake Without Rattles Bites 86-Year-Old Cleveland County Woman; Santa Monica Update: Philip Is Fine
summary: An 86-year-old Kingsland woman is recovering after a juvenile rattlesnake bit her near an azalea bush in Cleveland County. She drove herself for help and received four units of antivenom.
body:
I'm Philip Massouh, and this is SnakeNews.

Stop what you're doing, because the snakes just changed the game in Cleveland County, Arkansas. For thirty-two years, Shirley McGann walked the woods of South Arkansas for the Arkansas Forestry Commission, and for thirty-two years, the snakes slithered away and left her alone. That changed on November first, when an 86-year-old woman from Kingsland met a juvenile rattlesnake near an azalea bush, and the encounter has our entire SnakeNews newsroom rattled.

Here's what we know. McGann had cut back some bushes at her place in the Herbine community, and after church on November first, she went back to pick up limbs and do a little yard work. As she reached down to gather cuttings from an azalea bush right at the woods line, she felt a prick against the top of her foot near the ankle. At first she thought she had bumped into one of the cut limbs. Then she saw it—about ten to eleven inches of what she believed to be the tail of a small rattlesnake disappearing into the woods under the pine straw. No rattle. No warning. Just a juvenile snake with a bite that would send her to the hospital.

McGann did exactly what anyone in that terrifying moment would do: she kept her head. She made her way to some steps about fifty feet away and tried to call her son, who lives about a quarter-mile down the road. When he didn't answer, she got in her car and drove to his house. Then she laid on the horn in the driveway until her son and his wife came out. They moved fast, and soon she was on her way to Bradley County Medical Center in Warren. The family called ahead to let the emergency room know she had been bitten by what most likely was a rattlesnake.

Let that sink in. An 86-year-old woman, alone in the South Arkansas woods, bitten by a rattlesnake, and she drove herself to get help. That is the kind of grit that makes me proud to cover snake stories for a living. At first, McGann didn't feel much pain. But by the time they reached the hospital about thirty minutes after the bite, her leg was beginning to throb. Doctors gave her four units of antivenom. She stayed in the hospital through Tuesday. The swelling has gone down since then, and she is recovering—recovering, not because the snake was kind, but because she stayed calm and got to a hospital fast.

Now, here at the SnakeNews Safety Desk, our entire staff is hugging their ankles and looking at every azalea bush in a new light. The species in this case? We don't have a confirmation, but McGann, who spent decades in those woods, said the snake had no rattles—something you see in juvenile rattlesnakes before they develop that signature warning. A snake without a rattle doesn't mean a snake without venom. Rattlesnakes, especially juveniles, live in the pine woods and underbrush of South Arkansas, exactly where this bite happened: the tree line, the pine straw, the places where a bush meets the wild.

Here's what you do if a snake bites you, because the SnakeNews Safety Desk is not here to scare you, we're here to save you. Call 911 immediately. Stay calm. Keep the bitten limb still, ideally at or below heart level while you wait for help. Do not apply a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out venom. Those old cowboy tricks can make things worse. The real hero of this story is not just McGann; it's the calm, careful decision to get to a hospital and the antivenom that waited there.

And now, the SnakeNews Santa Monica check-in. I want to be very clear about this: I'm Philip Massouh, I'm in Santa Monica, and I am fine. The Pacific Ocean is still there. The palm trees are still swaying. Our newsroom has zero rattlesnake sightings, zero azalea bushes, and zero reason to panic. But if a snake ever does show up in Santa Monica, I want every one of you to remember this story from Cleveland County: stay calm, call for help, and drive to the hospital if you have to. That's the difference between a bad day and a tragedy.

Snakes are patient. They wait in the pine straw. They don't always have rattles. But the people who survive are the ones who keep their heads. Shirley McGann did, and that's why we're telling her story tonight as a recovery, not as something far worse.

I'm Philip Massouh. Stay snake aware.
